newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Creditanstalt bidders lose race against time.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Creditanstalt bidders lose race against time.

text.p: An Austro-Italian-German consortium of bidders for privatisation candidate Creditanstalt has failed to agree on a joint offer for the bank, a source close to the negotiations said on Friday.

The source said savings bank Die Erste had left the consortium and Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali was now working with its partners on a separate offer for the flagship of the Austrian banking sector.
"The consortium wanted to go it alone," the source told Reuters.
A spokesman for Creditanstalt confirmed the bank had been informed of Die Erste's departure from the consortium.

The group, which includes Banca Commerciale Italiana, Germany's Commerzbank and several Austrian companies, has been at odds over Die Erste's plans to form a joint holding with Creditanstalt which it would control.

Die Erste is barely a third the size of Creditanstalt, which boasts assets of almost 700 billion schillings ($67 billion) and has become one of the most successful players on the emerging markets of eastern and central Europe.
The negotiations, which have been mired in problems for several months, broke down just hours from an extended deadline imposed by Finance Minister Viktor Klima, who is in charge of the sale.
He has threatened to reopen the six-year privatisation process on Monday and invite new offers from other potential bidders if the consortium fails to agree on a common stance by midnight Friday.
"I have said very clearly that I expect an offer by midnight Friday," he told reporters.
None of the consortium members was available for offical comment on the reports, and an official in the Finance Ministry said the government had not yet been informed of the consortium's failure.
Earlier, the Vienna stock exchange suspended trade in Creditanstalt's ordinary and preferred shares as well as in EA-Generali's ordinary shares "pending an important announcement".
Die Erste had on Friday morning still appeared confident it could reach an agreement with its consortium partners.

"The board (of Die Erste) expects that it will succeed in meeting the deadline and sumbit an attractive offer by the consortium that will meet the conditions of the government," it said in a brief statement.

Klima has been pressing for a speedy conclusion to what has turned into Austria's longest-running privatisation saga, eager for the projected 18 billion schillings in revenue to help plug his growing budget holes.

Many international bidders, among them Germany's Allianz and CS Holding of Switzerland, have over the years lost interest in Creditanstalt, turned off by what they felt was a bias against foreigners in Austria.
Before suspension, Creditanstalt's ordinary shares were down eight schillings at 661 on the Vienna stock exchange, while its preference shares were down 6.10 schillings at 477.90.

The preferred shares -- 70 percent of which are held by the Republic of Austria, giving it 48.6 percent of the bank's base capital -- have fallen by as much as 23 percent over the past six months and are now hovering near their 1996 low of 470.30 schillings, reached at the end of August. ($1=10.44 Schilling)
